source_text: Ὥσπερ δὲ κτῆμα τὸ ἐξ ἁρπαγῆς βλαβερώτατον καὶ ἀνοσιώτατον, οὕτω καὶ ἀνδρὶ ἐπιθυμητῇ χρημάτων οὐκ ἐκγίνεται κόρος, οὔθ᾽ ἡ παρὰ τῶν πέλας εὔνοια· κἂν ὁτιοῦν μάλιστα πάμπολυ ἀργύριον ἐπικτήσωνται. Τοῦτο μὲν γὰρ μάταιον. Ἀγαθότης δὲ τοὺς συνόντας αὐτῇ ὑπερευφραίνουσα, ἀνδρείους ἀπεργάζεται τοῦ καθορᾶν ἕκαστα τῶν πραγμάτων παρέχουσα τὴν δύναμιν. Μέγα δὲ καὶ τὸ μὴ προστετηκέναι τοιαύταις φροντίσιν· ὁ μέν γε πένης, κἂν δοῦλος ᾖ, καὶ μὴ ὑπερεμπλήσας τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γαστέρα, προσηνοῦς μεταλαμβάνει τῆς διὰ τοῦ ὕπνου ἀνέσεως· πλούτου δὲ ἐπιθυμία σύνεστι ἀγρυπνίαις καὶ καμάτοις ψυχῆς. Τί δ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο τούτου ἀτοπώτερον, ἢ τὸ μετὰ πολλῆς σπουδῆς καὶ ἐπιμελείας ἀποθησαυρίζοντα τὸν πλοῦτον συντηρεῖν, μυρίων ἑαυτῷ φυλάσσοντα κακῶν ἀφορμήν; Καὶ τὸν πλοῦτον ἐκεῖνον ἀνάγκη ἀπολέσθαι ποτὲ καὶ διαφθαρῆναι, εἴτε γένοιτο τῷ κτησαμένῳ τέκνα, εἴτε καὶ μή· αὐτόν τε εἰ καὶ μὴ βούλοιτο προσήκει τοιοῦτον εἰς τὴν γῆν πεσεῖν καὶ ἀπελθεῖν, οἷος καὶ ὁπότε εἰς τὸ εἶναι παρὼν ἐτύγχανε. Κεναῖς δὲ χερσὶν ἀπιέναι μέλλων, αὔξει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κακίαν, ὥσπερ οὐκ ἐνθυμούμενος, ὅτι ἐπίκειται αὐτῷ τέλος τοῦ βίου τῇ γενέσει ὅμοιον, καὶ ὅτι ἀνόνητα μοχθεῖ, εἰς δέ τινα μᾶλλον ἀνέμου ὁρμήν, ἤπερ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σπουδῇ χαριζόμενος, καταναλώσας τὸν ἑαυτοῦ βίον σύμπαντα, ἔν τε ἐπιθυμίαις ἀνοσιωτάταις, καὶ ἐν ὁρμαῖς ἀλόγοις, ἔτι δὲ λύπαις καὶ ἀρρωστίαις. Καὶ συνελόντι φάναι, σκότος μέν εἰσι τῷ τοιούτῳ αἱ ἡμέραι· πένθος δὲ ἡ ζωή. Ἀγαθόν γε μὴν ἐκεῖνο καὶ οὐκ ἀπόβλητον· Θεοῦ γάρ ἐστι δῶρον, τὸ δυνηθῆναι ἀπολαῦσαι ἄνθρωπον τῶν ἑαυτοῦ καματῶν ἐν εὐφροσύνῃ, θεόσδοτα, καὶ οὐχ ἁρπακτικὰ δεξάμενον κτήματα. Οὔτε γὰρ λύπαις οὖτός γε νοσεῖ, οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐνθυμήσεσι πονηραῖς δουλεύει· συμμετρεῖται δὲ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ βίον εὐποιίαις τοῖς πᾶσιν εὐθυμούμενος, καὶ ἀγαλλιώμενος τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ δωρεᾷ.
thought_title: Wealth never satisfies; enjoyment is God's gift
orientation: Greed never satisfies, but to enjoy honest labor with gladness is a gift of God.
pass_a_gloss: As a possession from robbery is most harmful and most unholy, so to a man desirous of money no satiety arises, nor the goodwill of neighbors, even if they acquire however very much silver. For this is vain. Goodness, gladdening exceedingly those who are with it, makes them manly/strong, providing the power to see clearly each of the affairs. Great also is not to cling to such cares; the poor man, even if he is a slave and has not overfilled his belly, partakes of the gentle rest through sleep; but desire of wealth is joined with sleeplessness and toils of soul. What could be more absurd than, with much eagerness and care, treasuring up wealth, to keep it, guarding for oneself a starting-point of countless evils? And that wealth must some time perish and be destroyed, whether children are born to the one who acquired it or not; and he himself, even if he does not wish, must fall to the earth and depart such as he was when he came into being. About to depart with empty hands, he increases his own wickedness, as though not considering that there lies upon him an end of life like his birth, and that he toils profitlessly, gratifying a rush of wind rather than his own effort, having spent his whole life in most unholy desires and irrational impulses, and further in griefs and sicknesses. To sum up, darkness are the days to such a man, mourning the life. Good, however, is that and not to be rejected: for it is God's gift that a man be able to enjoy his own labors in gladness, having received God-given and not rapacious possessions. For this man neither is sick with griefs, nor for much is enslaved to evil thoughts; he measures out his life with good deeds to all, being cheerful and exulting in God's gift.

pass_b_english: Just as a possession seized by robbery is most harmful and most unholy, so the man who craves money never has his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of his neighbors, even if such men gain ever so vast a sum of silver (Ecclesiastes 5:10). For this is vain. But goodness gladdens beyond measure those who keep company with it and makes them strong, granting them the power to see each thing clearly (Ecclesiastes 5:11). It is a great thing, too, not to cling to such cares. The poor man, even if he is a slave and has not stuffed his belly full, enjoys the gentle rest that sleep brings; but the desire for wealth lives with sleepless nights and weariness of soul (Ecclesiastes 5:12). What could be more absurd than to hoard up wealth with great effort and care and keep it safe, guarding for oneself the source of countless evils (Ecclesiastes 5:13)? That wealth must one day perish and be destroyed, whether its owner has children or not (Ecclesiastes 5:14). And he himself, even if he does not wish it, must fall to the earth and depart just as he was when he first came into being (Ecclesiastes 5:15).

As he is about to depart with empty hands, he adds to his own wickedness, as if he did not consider that an end of life like his birth lies before him, and that he toils for nothing, serving some gust of wind rather than his own purpose (Ecclesiastes 5:16), after spending his whole life in most unholy desires and senseless impulses, and in griefs and sicknesses besides (Ecclesiastes 5:17). In short, for such a man the days are darkness and life is mourning. Yet this is good and not to be cast aside, for it is a gift of God: that a person can enjoy his own labors with gladness, having received possessions given by God and not seized by robbery (Ecclesiastes 5:18-19). For such a man is not sick with griefs, nor is he much enslaved to evil thoughts; he measures out his life in good deeds toward all, glad of heart and rejoicing in the gift of God (Ecclesiastes 5:20).
notes: Verse citations use English numbering; Gregory follows the LXX/Hebrew division, in which these verses are 5:9-19. Read with κόρος ('satiety') as printed in the source row (corrected from the transcription's χόρος). 'Goodness ... makes them strong ... the power to see' reworks LXX 5:10, where ἀγαθωσύνη ('goods'), ἀνδρεία ('advantage') and ὁρᾶν ('to see') stand; Gregory turns 'goods' into the virtue of goodness. 'Serving some gust of wind rather than his own purpose' renders εἰς ... ἀνέμου ὁρμήν ... ἤπερ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ σπουδῇ χαριζόμενος: his toil gratifies the wind rather than his own effort (LXX 5:15 'he toils for the wind'). 'Nor is he much enslaved' renders οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ, echoing LXX 5:19 'he will not much remember the days of his life'. 'In good deeds toward all' takes τοῖς πᾶσιν with εὐποιίαις; it could instead go with εὐθυμούμενος ('cheerful in all things').
